title: Introduction: Why AI Changes Investment Analysis
description: Professional-grade investment research used to require a team and a Bloomberg terminal. AI has closed most of that gap. Here's the framework this series will teach you to use it well.
content:
Have you ever looked at a stock and thought, “this could be a great investment,” and then gotten stuck? Too many financial reports, too many competing opinions, no clear place to start. That stuck feeling isn’t a personal failing. It’s a resourcing problem. Professional investment analysis, the kind hedge funds and wealth managers do every day, has always required a team of analysts working for hours, sometimes days, on a single idea.
That’s changing. With AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, an individual investor can now replicate that same professional-grade analysis framework, alone, in a fraction of the time.
The problem AI actually solves Individual investors face a familiar set of obstacles:
Information overload. Too much data, not enough time to make sense of it. No starting point. Not knowing where to look or what actually matters. Emotional whiplash. FOMO on the way up, fear of losing money on the way down. Expensive tooling. Bloomberg terminals and professional research services were never built for a part-time individual investor. Professional analysts don’t face these obstacles because they have teams and expensive tools. Now, individual investors can have their own AI analyst team instead.
Here’s what AI is genuinely good at in this context:
Processing large amounts of information quickly Applying a structured analysis framework consistently Playing devil’s advocate: arguing against your own thesis to remove emotional bias Generating multiple perspectives on the same company And here’s what it doesn’t replace: your judgment, and the final decision. AI assists; you decide. That division of labor is the backbone of everything in this series.
Your AI toolkit You don’t need to master every AI tool before starting. This series will show you exactly how and when to use each one. As a preview:
ChatGPT: versatile, good at following complex prompts, general-purpose analysis and brainstorming. Claude: excels at deep reasoning and synthesizing complex information; useful for nuanced valuation and risk work. Perplexity: internet-connected and source-cited, ideal for recent news and fact-checking. NotebookLM: Google’s document-grounded research assistant; upload a 10-K or earnings transcript and get cited answers instead of guesses. Grok: real-time access to X (Twitter) and current market data, useful for sentiment and technical checks. Free tiers exist for all of them, though the paid versions are worth it if you’re doing this seriously.
The five-step framework Every article in this series maps to one stage of a five-step research process used by professional investment teams:
Screening: find opportunities worth a closer look Fundamental analysis: understand the business, its financials, and its competitive position Technical & sentiment check: assess whether the timing is right Bull/bear debate: challenge your own assumptions before you commit capital Decision & risk management: size the position, define the exit, and make the call Each step filters and refines your conviction. Skipping one is how good analysis turns into a bad decision. The point isn’t to find the perfect investment on your first pass, it’s to build a repeatable process that compounds in quality every time you use it.
By the end of this series, you’ll have a complete, reusable framework, plus the actual prompt templates, that takes you from “I think this might be interesting” to “here’s my investment thesis, my position size, and my exit plan.”
Let’s start where every professional analysis starts: inside an actual investment firm, watching how the process really works.

title: Welcome, fellow explorer
description: Begin your trading education journey with this introductory guide. Learn how to navigate the world of trading and investing through a structured, story-driven approach that builds practical skills and systems.
content:
The world of trading and investing can feel like a vast, uncharted wilderness. Some rush in without a map, chasing quick profits, only to get lost in the noise. Others spend years collecting knowledge, yet never turn it into a practical system they can trust.
This blog series was designed to change that.
Instead of overwhelming readers with random theories or endless technical jargon, we take you on a guided storytelling journey - like an explorer’s handbook. Each post is a step forward on the path, where we’ll:
Discover the landscape of trading and investing Equip ourselves with essential tools and survival skills Build a personal learning system tailored to our style By the end, we won’t just “know more” about trading. We’ll have started shaping our own learning journey, a path we can continue to walk long after we finish reading.
It’s a compass and toolkit for those ready to answer the call to adventure - to grow from a curious beginner into a resilient, skilled trader.
Let’s begin the journey.

title: How Investment Firms Actually Work
description: A walk through a single day at a fictional investment firm (screening, deep research, the investment committee debate, and the decision framework) to see where structure, not prediction, does the work.
content:
The firm and characters below are fictitious. It’s a teaching case designed to show how professional investors actually work. The process is real.
Most people assume professional investors have some secret sauce, a magical ability to predict the future. They don’t. What they have is structure: a defined process they run every single time, regardless of how excited or nervous they feel about an idea. Here’s what that process looks like over the course of one day at a fictional firm, Aurexum Capital, as a senior analyst named Marcus evaluates a new opportunity for portfolio manager Emma.
9:00 AM | Screening: separating signal from noise With thousands of publicly traded companies, Marcus doesn’t pick stocks randomly. Every week he runs a screening process, a set of filters (revenue growth, margins, valuation, industry tailwinds) that narrows the universe down to 10–15 companies worth a closer look. Most candidates fail the filters immediately; that’s the point.
The ones that pass get a 30-minute “sniff test”: does the business model make sense, are the financials clean, are there obvious red flags? Only after clearing that initial check does Marcus commit real time to deep analysis. No emotional attachment, just process. Screening isn’t about finding the perfect investment on the first try. It’s about finding companies worth analyzing at all.
11:00 AM | Deep research: building a mosaic Deep research happens in layers, not as a single pass:
Financial statements: three to five years of income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow trends. Is revenue growing consistently? Are margins expanding or contracting? Is the company generating real cash, not just accounting profit? Competitive positioning: market share, customer retention, switching costs. Amateurs look at a company in isolation; professionals always look at competitive context. Valuation: multiple approaches (P/E, DCF, historical averages, peer multiples) to determine whether the stock is cheap, expensive, or fair. Technical and sentiment: what is the market actually telling you right now? Volume, key support/resistance levels, analyst sentiment, news flow. Each layer adds a piece to the picture. None of them alone is the answer. It’s the combination that builds the case, which Marcus then writes up as a research memo: bull case, bear case, risks, and catalysts.
2:00 PM | The investment committee: attacking your own idea At 2 PM, Marcus presents his thesis to the investment committee. Emma’s first response isn’t “great, let’s do it.” It’s “now tell me why we shouldn’t invest.” The team doesn’t try to sell each other on the idea; they try to break it. They stress-test assumptions: what happens if a major customer is lost? What if the sector is late-cycle? Marcus has to defend the thesis point by point.
This is deliberate. Bad ideas die in this room. Good ideas get better. Arguing against your own thesis before committing capital is what protects the firm from costly mistakes, and it’s the single habit individual investors skip most often.
3:30 PM | From analysis to decision Analysis tells you what might happen. A decision framework tells you what to do about it. Before entering any position, Emma answers three questions:
How much? Position sizing reflects conviction. A 1% position signals low conviction; 5–7% is a meaningful bet; anything larger demands exceptional conviction and limited downside. At what price? Liking a company isn’t the same as buying it at any price. Entry needs a defined trigger, whether that’s a technical level, a catalyst, or a valuation threshold. What could go wrong? Stop-losses and exit criteria are defined before entry, not improvised after the fact. That last point is the difference between investing and gambling: exit criteria before entry. Structure over prediction, process over outcomes. Professional firms don’t predict the future, they manage probabilities and take calculated risks with defined downside and asymmetric upside.
Where AI fits in What Marcus did in one day (screening, deep research, competitive analysis, valuation, a research memo, and a defended thesis) adds up to six-plus hours of skilled work. Most individual investors either skip it entirely or spend weeks trying to replicate it alone.
AI changes that math. The same five-step framework Aurexum Capital runs internally maps directly onto AI tools:
Screening: AI scans and filters companies against criteria you define. Fundamental analysis: AI reads financial statements, explains business models, and benchmarks competitors, citing its sources. Technical & sentiment: AI interprets charts and summarizes market sentiment from news and social media. Bull/bear debate: you can prompt AI to argue both sides. You become your own investment committee. Decision & risk management: AI helps structure your decision framework and stress-test your assumptions. The playing field isn’t leveling completely. You still won’t have insider access or institutional resources. But the analytical process, the structured thinking, the discipline that separates Marcus and Emma’s decision from a coin flip? That’s now accessible to anyone willing to learn how to use these tools well.
The next article breaks down the full five-step workflow in detail, before we start applying it step by step.

title: How to Thrive and Succeed in Trading
description: Learn why most traders fail and discover the structured approach needed to thrive in markets through discipline and process over quick profits.
content:
The market is like a jungle - with the right guidebook, every trail becomes a discovery.
Introduction Picture this: someone has just opened their first trading account. Charts are flashing, prices moving, and with one click they can buy or sell. They feel excited - maybe even powerful.
Fast forward six months… their account is bleeding, their confidence is gone, and they wonder if trading is just “not for them.”
This story is incredibly common.
In fact, studies suggest that 80-90% of retail traders lose money. Here’s the twist: many fail not because they’re not smart enough. They fail because they step into the jungle without a map, without survival tools, and without knowing the traps that lie ahead.
The Challenge Many beginners believe trading success comes from finding the “perfect” indicator or holy grail strategy, copying trades from social media gurus, or relying on luck and “gut feel.”
The truth? Many traders struggle because they underestimate the journey, treating trading like a quick win rather than a disciplined profession. This mindset, combined with other challenges like market unpredictability, often sets them up for losses.
Common traps that catch traders include overleveraging by risking too much on one trade, having a lack of risk management by ignoring stop-losses or proper position sizing, falling into emotional trading patterns like chasing losses or overtrading, and developing shiny object syndrome by hopping from strategy to strategy without achieving mastery. These behaviors can both cause losses and create a feedback loop that’s tough to break without discipline.
Key Insights Here are the core lessons every new trader must absorb early to set themselves up for long-term success.
Trading is fundamentally a skill, not a gamble. Just like learning chess, piano, or medicine, mastery takes years, not weeks. Those who expect quick riches almost always burn out before they develop the patience and consistency needed for sustainable profits. The traders who thrive approach it as a craft to be developed over time.
At the beginning of any trading journey, survival matters more than profits. The first mission isn’t to double an account overnight. It’s to stay in the game long enough to learn. Account blow-ups end the journey before it truly begins. Protecting capital and building experience should be the primary focus in those crucial early months and years.
The roadmap and system matter far more than raw intelligence or natural talent. A trader who follows a clear system with strict risk rules will consistently outperform someone who might be “smarter” but trades chaotically.
Closing Thought Many traders stumble not because the markets are unbeatable, but because they haven’t built the skills and habits needed for a disciplined journey. Approaching trading like an explorer with patience, preparation, and a clear map will set us apart from the crowd.
The market consistently rewards patience, discipline, and systematic thinking. It just as consistently punishes impatience, greed, and emotional decision-making. We’ll learn how to master these good habits in this learning journey.

title: The AI-Assisted Investment Workflow, Step by Step
description: The complete five-step research framework, walked through end-to-end on a single hypothetical idea, plus exactly where AI fits into each step and where your own judgment has to take over.
content:
Professional firms rarely deviate from a set process. That’s not because creativity doesn’t matter, but because a repeatable process is what separates a good decision that happens to lose money from a bad decision that happens to make it. This article lays out the complete five-step framework this series follows, walks through how one idea flows from step to step, and shows exactly where AI does the heavy lifting versus where you have to.
The five-step framework Step Question it answers Output 1. Screening & Idea Generation “What’s interesting right now?” 3–5 candidates worth investigating 2. Fundamental Analysis “Is this a good business at a reasonable price?” Investment thesis based on fundamentals 3. Technical & Sentiment Check “Is now a good time to enter?” Entry/exit considerations, risk level 4. Bull/Bear Debate “What could go wrong? What could go right?” A balanced view with risks identified 5. Decision & Risk Management “How much capital, and when do I exit?” A trade plan: entry, exit, position size Each step filters and refines your conviction. Like a prosecutor building a case, you need all the evidence, not just the evidence that supports the conclusion you already wanted.
Watching it flow through one idea Imagine it’s Q4 2024 and AI infrastructure spending is dominating headlines.
Step 1: Screening. Criteria: AI infrastructure companies, revenue growth above 20%, market cap above $100B. NVIDIA, AMD, Microsoft, and Google surface. NVIDIA shows the strongest momentum, so it advances to fundamental analysis.
Step 2: Fundamental analysis. Revenue is growing explosively in the data center segment, gross margins are industry-leading at roughly 70%, and the CUDA software ecosystem creates real switching costs. The one flag: the stock trades at roughly 50x earnings. Expensive, but is it justified by growth? Strong fundamental case, with valuation as a clear risk factor to carry forward.
Step 3: Technical & sentiment. The chart shows a strong uptrend breaking to all-time highs. Sentiment on social media and among analysts is extremely bullish. Momentum is real, but so is the risk of an overcrowded trade, so position sizing should account for that.
Step 4: Bull/bear debate. Bull case: the AI revolution is just getting started, and NVIDIA’s moat gives it years of dominance. Bear case: valuation is stretched, and competition from AMD and hyperscalers’ custom chips is a real threat. Synthesis: high conviction in the business, moderate concern about valuation and timing.
Step 5: Decision & risk management. Buy, but with a 2–3% portfolio allocation, smaller than a high-conviction position, reflecting the valuation risk. Scale in over two to three weeks. Stop-loss 15% below entry. Hold long-term, trim if valuation stretches past 60x earnings.
Notice what happened: each step informed the next. Screening didn’t decide the investment. It just earned NVIDIA the right to be analyzed further. The valuation flag from Step 2 shaped the position-sizing decision in Step 5. That’s the power of running the full framework instead of cherry-picking the steps that feel most interesting.
Why structure beats prediction Nobody, not even the most successful professional investor, can consistently predict where a stock price will be next month. What they do instead is assess probabilities and manage risk. Structure protects you from the cognitive biases that quietly wreck individual decision-making:
Confirmation bias: only seeking information that supports the view you already hold Recency bias: overweighting whatever just happened Anchoring: fixating on a past price as if it were meaningful FOMO: letting the fear of missing out drive an impulsive decision A structured process forces you to look at opposing viewpoints (the bull/bear debate), separates analysis from emotion, and creates a documented trail you can actually learn from later. A good decision with a bad outcome is still a good decision. If unexpected news moves the stock against you, that’s not a failure of process. Over time, good process compounds into better results, the same way a pilot’s pre-flight checklist doesn’t guarantee a smooth flight but reliably prevents the same category of mistake.
Where AI fits into each step Step What AI does What you do Screening Filters thousands of stocks against criteria instantly Define the criteria, judge the quality of results Fundamental analysis Reads financial statements, explains business models, benchmarks competitors Interpret business quality, verify outputs Technical & sentiment Describes chart patterns, aggregates news sentiment Assess the risk/reward setup, filter noise Bull/bear debate Generates comprehensive arguments on both sides Weigh the arguments, judge which risks matter most Decision & risk management Calculates position sizing, suggests risk parameters Make the final call based on your own risk tolerance AI is a tireless research assistant: it never gets tired, never gets emotional, and can hold several perspectives at once. What it can’t do is predict the future, account for a genuine black-swan event, understand your personal financial situation, or take responsibility for the outcome. AI brings speed, breadth, and objectivity. You bring context, judgment, and the final decision.
The next five articles walk through each step in depth, using a real company as a running example so you can see exactly how the prompts and the reasoning work in practice.

title: Defining Your 'Why' in Trading & Investing
description: Discover how defining a clear purpose beyond money becomes the anchor that keeps us persistent through market challenges and setbacks.
content:
Every great adventure begins with a powerful reason to leave home. This reason becomes our North Star in our adventure.
Introduction Imagine two explorers setting out on a dangerous expedition. One goes because he’s curious, the other because his family’s survival depends on it. When the path gets rough, who’s more likely to push through?
Trading and investing are no different. Most people start with vague motives: “I want to make money” or “I want freedom.” But vague reasons collapse the moment challenges appear. Defining a clear “why” gives traders an anchor that keeps them going when the market tests them.
The Challenge Many beginners skip this step entirely. They jump straight into charts, brokers, and hot stock tips, without ever asking: “Why am I really doing this?”
The result is predictable. Instead of building required skills first, they chase profits with no deeper purpose, fall into comparison by trading just because others seem to succeed, and quit after a big loss.
Without a strong “why,” the market feels like a storm with no compass.
Key Insights Here are some key insights about finding and maintaining motivation in trading.
Money alone is not enough to sustain a trading career. Money is a result, not a reason. If the only motivation is “get rich,” setbacks may be more difficult to overcome. Real traders build around deeper values like freedom, mastery, or contribution to others. These deeper motivations provide the resilience we need for long-term success.
A trader’s why shapes their trading style. Someone trading for time freedom won’t choose the same path as someone aiming for intellectual challenge or wealth compounding. The motivation determines the method: day trading for quick results, swing trading for balance, or long-term investing for steady growth.
The why becomes a compass during difficult times. When we are tempted by distractions like new strategies or social media hype, a clear why brings us back to our chosen path. It acts as a filter for decision-making and helps maintain focus on what truly matters.
While skills like risk management are important, a strong “why” is the invisible force that supports our persistence and resilience.
Closing Thought Defining a clear “why” is the first piece of armor in any trading journey. It won’t guarantee profits, but it will guarantee persistence when the inevitable challenges arise.

title: Step 1: Screening & Idea Generation
description: How to filter thousands of stocks down to a handful worth real analysis, the prompt templates that do it, and how to tell a good AI screening result from a lazy one.
content:
Screening is the process of filtering the investment universe to identify opportunities worth deeper investigation. With 4,000+ stocks on US exchanges alone, you can’t analyze everything. You need a filter, and the professional approach is to start broad and narrow systematically.
It helps to separate two related habits: scanning is passive awareness (reading news, tracking sectors), while screening is active filtering against specific criteria. Scanning generates ideas; screening validates them. You need both, but screening is what turns a vague hunch into a shortlist.
What to screen for Screening criteria generally fall into four buckets:
Fundamental: market cap, revenue growth, profitability (margins, ROE), valuation ratios (P/E, P/S, PEG), debt levels Thematic/sector: industry, mega-trends (AI, renewable energy, aging population), geographic exposure Technical: price momentum, 52-week highs/lows, volume trends, moving averages Quality: analyst ratings, institutional ownership, insider buying or selling Where this used to require an expensive screener like Bloomberg or FactSet, AI can now do a reasonable first pass through plain conversation. The goal isn’t perfection. Be specific enough to filter, broad enough not to miss opportunities (“AI infrastructure stocks” rather than “companies with exactly 23.5% revenue growth”). Screening generates candidates, not final decisions. You’re aiming for 3–5 companies to investigate further, not 100.
The screening prompt I'm looking for investment opportunities in [SECTOR/THEME]. Please help me screen for companies with the following criteria: - [Criterion 1: e.g., Market cap > $50B] - [Criterion 2: e.g., Revenue growth > 20% YoY] - [Criterion 3: e.g., Operating margins > 15%] - [Criterion 4: e.g., Strong competitive positioning] For each company, provide: 1. Ticker symbol and company name 2. Why it meets the criteria 3. One potential concern or risk Limit to top 5 candidates. The structure matters: context (what you’re looking for and why), specific and quantifiable criteria where possible, an explicit output format, and a limit so you don’t get overwhelmed with results.
A few useful variations, depending on what kind of idea you’re chasing:
Thematic screening: “I want to find companies positioned to benefit from [TREND]. Criteria: direct exposure (not tangential), established companies, strong financial position, positive analyst consensus. Provide 3–5 top ideas with brief rationale.”
Comparative screening: “I’m interested in companies similar to [COMPANY] in business model, growth profile, and market position, but trading at more attractive valuations. Suggest 3–4 alternatives with comparison points.”
Quality-at-a-reasonable-price screening: “Find me profitable companies with strong balance sheets, reasonable valuation (P/E below sector average), and a recent pullback of 10–20% from highs. Focus on large-caps for stability.”
Worked example: screening for AI infrastructure It’s Q4 2024, and AI is dominating headlines. The prompt used:
I'm looking for investment opportunities in AI infrastructure, companies that provide the hardware and computing power that enables AI applications. Please screen for companies with these criteria: - Market cap > $100B (established companies) - Revenue growth > 25% year-over-year - Strong competitive moat (hard to replicate technology) - Exposure to both consumer and enterprise markets For each company, provide: 1. Ticker and name 2. Why it fits AI infrastructure theme 3. Key financial metric that stands out 4. One concern or risk Top 5 candidates please. The response surfaces five names: NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Taiwan Semiconductor. Each is a defensible AI infrastructure play. NVIDIA stands out from the group for a specific reason: it’s the purest play (versus the diversified cloud giants), it shows the highest revenue growth among the candidates, and it has the clearest direct exposure to the AI trend through its CUDA software moat. The AI response also flags a concern worth carrying forward, the valuation premium versus historical averages, which becomes the seed of the fundamental analysis in the next step.
All five candidates are worth knowing about. NVIDIA simply shows the strongest momentum and the purest exposure to the theme, which is why it advances. Screening isn’t the investment decision. It’s the reason one candidate gets more of your time than the other 3,999 stocks you didn’t screen for.
Judging the quality of a screening result Not every AI screening response is equally useful. Run through this checklist before treating the result as a real shortlist:
Relevance: do the companies actually fit your stated criteria and sector? If AI returns companies that clearly don’t match, your prompt was too vague. Diversity: are you getting genuine variety, or five nearly identical companies (a sign your criteria were over-specified)? Data recency: ask directly: “when is this data from?” For fast-moving sectors, anything older than six months may be stale; use Perplexity to check current status if needed. Ticker verification: always confirm ticker symbols independently. AI can hallucinate or use outdated symbols. Balance: did the response include concerns as well as strengths? If everything is bullish with no risks mentioned, re-prompt explicitly asking for risks. Common failure modes and their fixes: too many results (criteria too broad; tighten or cap the output), too few or none (criteria too restrictive; relax one at a time), generic descriptions (ask for specific products or metrics), or outdated information (ask the AI to search the web, or switch to Perplexity).
Before moving on, do a quick verification pass on your top candidate: confirm the company and ticker are real, skim recent news for anything alarming, and check that it actually aligns with your own goals and expertise. If that all checks out, you’re ready for the next step: fundamental analysis.

title: Embracing the Learning Curve in Trading
description: Understand the realistic 2-5 year timeline for trading mastery and why focusing on skill development matters more than immediate profits.
content:
Trading is simple, but not easy - the challenge is about staying the course until the puzzle begins to make sense.
Introduction We have been studying charts for months, watched endless YouTube videos, even tried a paid course. We place trades, some win, some lose, but our account doesn’t really grow. Frustration creeps in. We wonder, “Am I missing something? Why does it feel like everyone else is ahead of me?”
The truth is that, we’re not failing. We’re on the hidden learning curve of trading. Every trader goes through it, but few talk about how long, messy, and non-linear it really is.
The Challenge Most beginners think trading success looks like this: learn some strategies, start trading, then profit consistently.
In reality, the curve looks more like this: Early excitement → Painful losses → False confidence → Long plateau → Gradual breakthroughs → Consistency.
The challenge is that most people quit during the plateau phase, mistaking “slow progress” for “no progress.”
Key Insights Here’s what we need to know about the hidden curve that defines this journey.
It takes years, not months, to master trading skill. Realistically, it takes 2–5 years for most traders to become consistently profitable. Like developing expertise in fields such as medicine or engineering, trading mastery often requires years of practice, mistakes, and reflection. While timelines may vary due to factors like market conditions or prior experience, expecting faster results can amplify risks, lead to disappointment and increase the likelihood of giving up.
Progress is often invisible at first. Traders may not see results in their account balance for a long time, but skills are growing beneath the surface. The skills like discipline, pattern recognition, and emotional control take time to build. These invisible improvements are the foundation that eventually supports profitable trading.
Everyone has a different learning curve. Some learn faster, some slower, depending on time, resources, and mindset. Comparing progress to others only fuels frustration and can lead to poor decision-making. We must focus on our own journey and timeline.
Closing Thought The learning curve in trading is long, hidden, and often painful, but that’s what makes the rewards so meaningful. If we set realistic expectations and stay the course, we’ll outlast most who quit too soon.

title: Step 2: Fundamental Analysis
description: Turning AI into a research analyst: reading financial statements, mapping the competitive moat, and checking valuation, with the role-playing prompts and a NotebookLM workflow that make it work.
content:
Fundamental analysis evaluates a company’s intrinsic value by examining its business model, financial health, competitive position, and growth prospects. The core question it answers: is this a good business at a reasonable price?
It rests on three pillars:
Business quality: what does the company do, who are its customers, what’s its moat, who are its competitors, what drives growth? Financial health: revenue trajectory, profitability, cash flow generation, balance sheet strength, return on invested capital Valuation: price relative to earnings, sales, and growth; comparison to peers and history A few misconceptions worth discarding up front: you don’t need to be an accounting expert (basic financial literacy is enough), you don’t need to predict exact future earnings (focus on trends and probabilities), expensive isn’t automatically bad and cheap isn’t automatically good, and you don’t need proprietary data, since public filings contain most of what you need. AI can read a 10-K in seconds and benchmark it against competitors, work that used to take analysts days.
By the end of this step, you should be able to state a clear investment thesis: “I believe [Company] is a [good/poor] investment because [3–4 key reasons].”
NotebookLM for document-grounded research Before diving into prompts, one tool deserves special mention: NotebookLM, Google’s free AI research assistant built specifically for working with your own documents. Unlike a general chat assistant, NotebookLM only uses the sources you upload. Every answer comes with a citation back to the exact document, which means it can’t hallucinate information that isn’t in your sources.
For fundamental analysis, that makes it ideal for company filings: upload a 10-K, the latest earnings transcript, and an investor presentation, then ask direct questions like “explain the company’s business segments and how the revenue mix has changed over the past two years” or “what does management say about competition, and what are the disclosed risk factors?” You get specific, cited answers instead of a general impression, turning hours of reading a 200-page filing into minutes of targeted questions. Use NotebookLM for deep, document-grounded facts; use ChatGPT or Claude for synthesis and role-playing analysis; use Perplexity when you need something more current than your uploaded documents.
Role-playing prompts Asking AI to adopt a specific analytical role produces more structured, professional output than a generic question. It mimics how investment firms actually staff an analysis, with different perspectives checking each other.
Act as a [TYPE] analyst with 10 years of experience covering the [SECTOR] sector. I want you to analyze [COMPANY NAME] and provide: 1. [Specific analysis request] 2. [Specific analysis request] 3. [Specific analysis request] Be specific with numbers and examples. Identify both opportunities and risks. Useful variations to run in sequence, each surfacing a different angle:
Fundamental equity analyst: business model, competitive advantages and threats, financial health, three bull points and three bear points, fair value versus current price. Growth investor: total addressable market and share, growth sustainability, margin expansion potential, key drivers for the next 2–3 years. Value investor (Buffett-style): durability of the moat, management and capital allocation quality, free cash flow and ROE, margin of safety at current price. Risk-focused analyst: business, financial, operational, and external risks, ranked by likelihood and impact. For comprehensive coverage in one pass, ask for all three lenses at once and a synthesis: “Give me the growth analyst view, the value analyst view, and the risk analyst view, each with an overall assessment, 3 supporting points, and the biggest concern. Then synthesize a balanced view.”
Worked example: NVIDIA’s fundamentals Financial statements. A prompt asking for three years of trend analysis on revenue, margins, cash flow, and balance sheet health surfaces a clear pattern: explosive revenue growth driven almost entirely by the data center segment, gross margins expanding from the low-60s into the low-70s as scale kicks in, near-100% conversion of earnings to free cash flow, and a fortress balance sheet with minimal debt. The green flags (expanding margins alongside explosive growth, exceptional cash generation) come with one yellow flag worth tracking: a single segment now represents the large majority of revenue. That’s a concentration risk rather than a red flag, but worth monitoring.
Competitive positioning. A “strategy consultant” prompt breaks down the moat: a 15-year software ecosystem (CUDA) with millions of trained developers, a full hardware-plus-software stack that’s hard for point-solution competitors to match, and high switching costs from rewriting code for an alternative platform. The most credible competitive threat isn’t the obvious rival (AMD, which has trailed for a decade). It’s hyperscalers building their own custom chips for internal workloads, which shrinks the addressable market rather than taking share directly.
Valuation. A valuation-specialist prompt compares current multiples to the company’s own five-year history and to peers, then runs bull/base/bear scenarios. The verdict is nuanced: expensive relative to history and most peers, but not obviously in bubble territory once growth is accounted for (a PEG ratio near 1 suggests the multiple is roughly in line with growth). The tension is real: strong business, strong position, but priced for continued excellence, which means limited room for disappointment.
Reading AI output critically AI-generated fundamental analysis is only as good as your verification of it. Run every response through a critical-reading checklist:
Verify the data. Check dates. Is this current or two years stale? Confirm key numbers against actual filings rather than trusting a stated percentage at face value. Check internal consistency. Does the response contradict itself (a “strong balance sheet” followed by a “high debt levels” claim)? Does the narrative hold together? Push past vague claims. “Strong market position” means nothing without a number. Ask directly: “what specific evidence supports that?” Watch for one-sided framing. AI tends toward positive framing by default. If a response reads as universally bullish, explicitly prompt for the bear case. Common AI errors to watch for: outdated training data (verify with Perplexity or fresh documents), plausible-sounding but invented metrics (verify anything unusually specific against real filings), oversimplified accounting (check whether a headline number includes a one-time item), and correlation dressed up as causation (“revenue grew because of AI”; dig into which specific products drove it).
The most reliable check is cross-referencing: run the same prompt through two different AI tools, and if they agree on the key facts, treat that as higher-confidence. If they disagree, go to the primary source, the actual filing, to resolve it.
By the end of this step you should be able to write a two-to-three sentence synthesis: what you’re confident about, where the tools disagreed, and your resulting thesis. That thesis is the input to the next step: checking whether the timing is actually right to act on it.

title: The 5 Major Asset Classes Every Trader Must Know
description: Explore the five asset kingdoms that form the financial ecosystem and learn how equities, bonds, currencies, commodities, and alternatives interconnect.
content:
When we understand the land we walk on, every step becomes intentional.
Introduction Imagine a traveler setting foot in a vast kingdom without a map. They see mountains, rivers, forests, and deserts, but don’t know which paths lead to treasures and which to traps.
That’s exactly how many beginners enter the financial markets. They hear buzzwords like “stocks,” “forex,” or “crypto,” but can’t see how these pieces fit together. Without this map, traders often jump blindly into a single market, unaware of how it connects to the bigger financial world.
Understanding the five major asset classes is like having a compass. It doesn’t just tell us where we are, it reveals the entire landscape we’re exploring.
The Challenge Most new traders make two critical mistakes:
They only know one kingdom. For example, they only trade stocks but have no idea how bonds or commodities affect them.
They chase hype without understanding fundamentals. Many rush into crypto or forex without understanding how different asset classes behave and interact.
This increases their risk of being blindsided. For example, a stock trader who overlooks bond yields, a forex trader who ignores commodity prices, or a crypto trader unaware of global liquidity flows might miss critical market signals.
In reality, all asset classes are connected, and knowing the basics of each provides a significant strategic advantage.
Key Insights Here are some foundational concepts about the asset class landscape that we should understand.
Each asset class serves a different economic function and responds to different fundamental drivers.
Equities are ownership stakes in companies and are driven by earnings, innovation, and investor sentiment. When Apple reports stronger-than-expected earnings due to strong iPhone sales, its stock price naturally rises, reflecting investor optimism about the company’s future prospects.
Fixed income is debt and borrowing, with interest rates as the primary driver. When US Treasury yields rise, it often puts pressure on stock markets as capital flows toward safer, more stable returns in bonds. These two classes often move inversely to each other.
Currency markets reflect the relative strength of nations and their economies through exchange rates like EUR/USD or GBP/JPY. When the Federal Reserve announces interest rate hikes, the US dollar typically strengthens as higher rates attract more international capital inflows.
Commodities are the raw materials like oil, gold, wheat, copper that power the global economy. During wars or political instability, oil prices often surge, triggering global inflation risks that affect all other asset classes.
Alternative assets offer diversification but come with unique risks and behaviors. Real estate, cryptocurrency, private equity, and other alternatives often move independently of traditional markets. Bitcoin’s concept as “digital gold” has attracted many investors, but its volatility far exceeds traditional assets.
The big idea is that each kingdom has its own rules, but together they form an interconnected financial ecosystem. Understanding these connections can help traders better anticipate market movements, though success also depends on factors like strategy, timing, and risk management.
Closing Thought Knowing asset classes is like knowing the kingdoms of a fantasy world. Each has its own culture, rules, and power dynamics. The best traders aren’t limited to one kingdom; they understand how the whole map works together.
When we master the basic knowledge of these five major asset classes, we gain essential tools for navigating financial markets. This not only helps make wiser trading decisions but also maintains clearer judgment during market volatility.
👉🏻 In the next chapter of this journey, we’ll meet the 4 Schools of Trading & Investing, the different philosophies that shape how traders navigate this vast landscape.

title: Step 3: Technical & Sentiment Check
description: Being right about a business isn't the same as being right about timing. How to use AI to read charts and gauge market sentiment before you commit capital, and how to treat extreme sentiment as a warning, not a green light.
content:
Fundamental analysis answers “what is the business worth?” Technical and sentiment analysis answers a different question: “what is the market willing to pay right now, and is momentum with you or against you?” You can be right about the fundamentals and still lose money if you buy at the wrong moment. A great company in a downtrend, breaking support, with negative sentiment, can put a fundamentally sound investor through a painful drawdown before being proven right.
Technical analysis tells you about trend (up, down, or sideways), key support and resistance levels, momentum, and whether a price move is backed by real volume. Sentiment analysis tells you about market psychology (is everyone bullish already, which is a contrarian warning, or bearish, which can be an opportunity?), crowding, news flow, and positioning. Together, they answer a narrower but important question than fundamentals do: not “should I own this,” but “is now a good time to buy, or should I wait?”
This is not day trading or an attempt to call the exact top or bottom. It’s simply asking whether the setup supports the thesis, or whether patience is the better move.
The technical analysis prompt Analyze the current technical setup for [TICKER: COMPANY NAME]. Provide: 1. Current trend - uptrend, downtrend, or sideways? 2. Key support and resistance levels 3. Recent price action - any breakouts, breakdowns, or consolidation? 4. Volume analysis - is the move supported by volume? 5. Technical indicators - RSI, moving averages, momentum 6. Overall assessment - bullish, bearish, or neutral setup? 7. Risk/reward - where to enter, where to place stop-loss? Use recent data (last 3-6 months) and be specific with price levels. A few things separate a useful response from a vague one: specific price levels (“support at $485”) instead of hand-waving (“support exists below”), appropriately hedged language (“likely,” not “will”), and volume included as part of the read, since a breakout on weak volume is a different signal than one on heavy volume. Treat overly confident predictions and analysis with no mention of a stop-loss level as red flags.
Worked example: NVIDIA’s technical setup With fundamental analysis complete (a strong business, but a demanding valuation), the technical read checks whether now is a good entry point. A prompt asking for trend, key levels, volume, indicators, and a stop-loss recommendation surfaces a nuanced picture: the uptrend is intact and healthy (higher highs, trading above both the 50-day and 200-day moving averages), but the stock is testing resistance after a strong six-week run, volume is weakening on the approach to that resistance level, and RSI is nearing overbought territory. The setup is bullish, but extended. The risk/reward at the current price is worse than it would be at a pullback to the nearest support level.
The takeaway isn’t “don’t buy NVIDIA.” It’s “the trend supports the thesis, but chasing the stock at resistance offers a poor risk/reward compared to waiting for either a pullback to support or a confirmed breakout on strong volume.”
The sentiment analysis prompt Analyze the current market sentiment for [TICKER: COMPANY NAME]. Provide: 1. News sentiment - what's the recent news flow? (positive/negative/neutral) 2. Social media sentiment - what are investors discussing? (bullish/bearish) 3. Analyst sentiment - recent upgrades/downgrades and price targets 4. Institutional positioning - are funds buying or selling? 5. Sentiment extreme check - is everyone too bullish or too bearish? 6. Contrarian signal - does sentiment suggest crowding or opportunity? Focus on the last 2-4 weeks for recency. This is where Grok earns a place in the toolkit: its integration with X gives it real-time access to social sentiment and current price action in a way that a general chat assistant, limited to its training-data cutoff, can’t match. A prompt like “what’s the current sentiment on X about [TICKER]? Are discussions bullish, bearish, or mixed, and how has that changed over the last week?” gives you a live read on crowd psychology. Perplexity is a solid alternative for news-flow and institutional-positioning questions if you don’t have Grok access.
Combining technical and sentiment: the synthesis that matters Running fundamental, technical, and sentiment analysis on NVIDIA together tells a more complete story than any one alone:
Analysis type Verdict Fundamental Strong business, reasonable valuation if growth continues Competitive Dominant position, moat defensible Technical Uptrend intact but extended, testing resistance Sentiment Extremely bullish across analysts, social media, and institutions; a crowded trade Sentiment sitting at an extreme is itself a signal, independent of the technical picture:
Extremely bullish (most sources agree): most potential buyers are already in, expectations are high, and the risk of disappointment rises. Contrarian read: be cautious. Extremely bearish: most potential sellers are already out, expectations are low, room for positive surprise. Contrarian read: possible opportunity, if fundamentals support it. Mixed: healthy debate, room to move either direction, often the best environment for new positions. The combination matters more than either signal alone: a strong uptrend backed by bullish sentiment is a case for continuation, but an uptrend that’s extended and sentiment that’s near-universally bullish is a caution flag. Everyone who was going to buy may have already bought, which raises the question of who’s left to push the price higher.
The verdict this step produces Technical and sentiment analysis don’t tell you whether to own a stock. Fundamentals do that. They tell you when, and at what price. A fundamentally excellent company can still be a “not yet” if the setup is extended and the crowd is already fully positioned. That’s not a rejection of the thesis. It’s patience, and it’s exactly the kind of discipline that separates a structured process from chasing whatever is trending this week.
With the business case, the timing check, and the sentiment read all in hand, the next step is the one professional firms treat as mandatory and individual investors most often skip: deliberately arguing against your own idea before you commit capital.

title: The 4 Schools of Trading & Investing (Which One Fits You?)
description: Discover the four trading philosophies (Fundamental, Technical, Quantitative, Hybrid) to find the approach that matches the personality and lifestyle.
content:
Every explorer carries a map - though the wilderness leads each one anew.
Introduction When most people think of trading or investing, they imagine one single path: “Buy low, sell high.”
But step into the financial world and the reality quickly becomes clear, there isn’t just one way to approach the markets. Some traders spend hours glued to charts. Others patiently hold for decades. Some crunch company reports, while others code algorithms.
Here’s the catch: beginners often try to mix everything at once - jumping from strategy to strategy - and end up lost in the wilderness.
That’s why it’s crucial to understand the 4 main schools of trading & investing. Each is like meeting a mentor with a different philosophy. Once we know them, we can decide: Which path feels right - at least for now?
The Challenge Many beginners make these critical mistakes:
Mixing philosophies by trying day trading one week, then long-term value investing the next. Copying others blindly by following a “guru” without realizing their style may not fit their lifestyle or risk tolerance. Ignoring personal fit by forgetting that time, capital, personality, and goals should guide the choice.
The truth is that there is no “best” school. Only the school that fits our current stage, resources, and personality.
Key Insights Here are the essential characteristics of each school and what makes them unique.
The Fundamental School represents “The Business Analyst” approach. These practitioners focus on company earnings, balance sheets, and economic trends. Their philosophy is simple: “Own great businesses, and value will show over time.” This includes value investing, growth investing, and long-term holdings. Famous practitioners include Warren Buffett and Peter Lynch.
The Technical School represents “The Chart Reader” methodology. Technical analysts focus on price charts, patterns, indicators, and volume data. Their core belief is: “Price reflects everything. Watch behavior, not opinions.” This approach powers day trading, swing trading, and momentum strategies. Notable figures include Jesse Livermore and Al Brooks.
The Quantitative School represents “The Mathematician” perspective. Quant traders rely on models, algorithms, probabilities, and data-driven strategies. Their governing principle: “Numbers don’t lie - systems over emotions.” This encompasses algorithmic trading, statistical arbitrage, and systematic fund management. Jim Simons of Renaissance Technologies exemplifies this approach.
The Hybrid/Philosophical School represents “The Synthesizer” philosophy. These traders combine different methods depending on market conditions. Their adaptive approach: “Use the right tool for the right job.” This includes macro investing, options strategies, and mixed approaches. George Soros and Ray Dalio exemplify this flexible methodology.
Closing Thought Choosing a trading school is like choosing a mentor at the start of an adventure. There’s no “best” choice, only the one that matches who we are today.
👉🏻 In the next chapter, we’ll discuss how to choose the first trading/investing path, so traders can move forward with clarity instead of confusion.

title: Step 4: The Bull/Bear Debate
description: Why professional firms force every idea through a devil's advocate before committing capital, how to make AI argue both sides with equal force, and how to synthesize the result into a real risk/reward number.
content:
Once you’ve formed an opinion about a stock, your brain starts working against you. Confirmation bias means you notice the news that supports your view and skim past the news that doesn’t. Anchoring means once you’ve decided a price is fair, you rationalize why it’s still fair even as conditions change. Overconfidence means you assume your analysis was thorough, which is rarely true.
Professional firms combat this structurally, not through willpower: analysts present the bull case and the bear case before a decision is made, someone is explicitly assigned to challenge the thesis, and an investment committee debates before capital moves. AI is a genuinely good devil’s advocate for this, precisely because it has no emotional attachment to being right. The same model that built your bull case can turn around and build an equally strong bear case, tirelessly, as many times as you ask.
The goal of this step isn’t to talk yourself out of a good idea. It’s to reveal blind spots you didn’t know you had, stress-test the thesis before the market does it for you, and, if the bull case survives serious challenge, walk away with genuinely higher conviction instead of borrowed confidence.
Building the strongest bull case The key instruction here is counterintuitive: don’t ask for a balanced case, ask for the strongest possible one. Balance comes later, in the synthesis step. Right now, self-censoring just produces a weaker analysis.
Act as a bullish analyst building the strongest possible investment case for [COMPANY]. Provide: 1. The core bull thesis in one sentence 2. 5-7 key reasons to be bullish (prioritized by importance) 3. What could go BETTER than current expectations? 4. Potential upside catalysts over the next 12-24 months 5. Base case and bull case price targets with assumptions 6. Why bears are wrong (counter the main bear arguments) Be specific with data and examples. This should be the STRONGEST possible bull case. A strong bull case has specific, quantifiable drivers rather than vague assertions, rests on multiple independent reasons rather than one load-bearing assumption, names plausible catalysts with a rough timeline, and still acknowledges risk while explaining why it’s manageable. Weak bull cases lean on a single dependency (“if AI grows, this stock wins”), assert qualities like “strong management” without evidence, or promise unrealistic upside that would require flawless execution and luck simultaneously.
For NVIDIA, a well-built bull case rests on several independent legs: AI infrastructure spending as a genuine multi-year trend rather than a fad, a CUDA software moat that’s taken 15 years to build and would be expensive for any customer to abandon, massive operating leverage as margins expand with scale, supply that’s currently more constrained than demand (a pricing-power signal), and a large untapped inference market beyond today’s training-focused revenue. None of these depends entirely on the others, which is exactly what makes a bull case robust rather than fragile.
Building the strongest bear case Then, deliberately, argue the other side, and take it just as seriously.
Act as a bearish analyst building the strongest possible case AGAINST investing in [COMPANY]. Provide: 1. The core bear thesis in one sentence 2. 5-7 key reasons to be bearish (prioritized by risk level) 3. What could go WORSE than current expectations? 4. Downside catalysts or triggers over the next 12-24 months 5. Bear case price target with assumptions 6. Why bulls are wrong (counter the main bull arguments) Be brutally honest. This should be the STRONGEST possible bear case - assume you're short the stock and need to convince others. A useful variant is the pre-mortem: “Imagine it’s two years from now and [COMPANY] has fallen 50%. What went wrong? What signs should we have seen coming? What did bulls miss?” Working backward from failure surfaces risks that a forward-looking prompt sometimes misses.
For NVIDIA, a serious bear case points to customer concentration (a handful of hyperscalers represent the majority of revenue, and they’re simultaneously building competing custom chips), the historical pattern of infrastructure cycles looking permanent right up until they aren’t, margins sitting at a cyclical high that historically mean-reverts, and a valuation that assumes several more years of uninterrupted execution with essentially no room for a miss.
The right emotional reaction to a good bear case is discomfort, not immediate rebuttal. If your first instinct is to argue with every point, you’re too anchored to the thesis already. The better question is “what if this is right, how would I know, and what would I do?”
Synthesizing both sides into a decision input Comparing the two cases side by side, rather than picking a winner outright, is the actual point of this exercise. For each side, ask three questions: which arguments are strongest, what has to be true for that case to win, and how likely is that?
A rough, explicit probability weighting turns two narratives into one number. For example: a bull scenario with 30% upside at 25–30% probability, a base case with -10% to -30% at roughly 50% probability, and a bear scenario with -40% to -58% at 15–20% probability, nets out to a probability-weighted expected return that can be mildly negative even when the bull case sounds compelling in isolation. That’s exactly the kind of thing narrative alone would hide from you.
That synthesis usually lands in one of four patterns:
Bull case wins clearly: upside meaningfully exceeds downside, bull dependencies more plausible than bear ones → larger position. Bear case wins clearly: downside meaningfully exceeds upside → avoid or exit. Mixed/uncertain (the most common outcome): both cases have real merit → small position, or wait for a better entry. Great company, wrong price: the long-term bull case is strong, but current valuation leaves no margin of safety → watchlist, wait for a pullback, or scale in slowly. Define your trip wires explicitly at this stage: the specific, observable events that would tell you the bear case is starting to play out (a named metric crossing a named threshold), not a vague feeling that “something’s off.” Writing them down now, while you’re not yet emotionally invested in the position, is what makes them usable later.
The most important question this step answers is simple: after hearing both sides, do I still want to own this? If yes, you move to the final step, turning that conviction into an actual position size and risk plan. If no, you’ve just avoided a mistake for free, and that’s a genuine win, not a wasted afternoon.

title: How to Choose Your First Trading/Investing Path
description: Learn to make a strategic first choice in trading approach based on the 'why,' lifestyle constraints, and risk tolerance rather than chasing trends.
content:
The first path doesn’t need to be perfect - it simply needs to begin.
Introduction Imagine standing at a crossroads. One path promises fast profits through day trading. Another whispers about steady long-term investing. A third tempts with options, leverage, and excitement. Many beginners freeze here, unsure which way to go.
This confusion isn’t surprising. The markets offer countless trading methods and investment strategies, each with supporters claiming their approach is superior. Faced with so many choices, it’s easy to fall into analysis paralysis.
The truth? Choosing the first trading/investing path is one of the most important decisions anyone will make in this journey. It shapes how we learn, what mistakes we face, and how we build confidence. The good news is that the path doesn’t need to be “perfect.” It just needs to be chosen wisely for where we are right now.
The Challenge Most beginners make two common mistakes when choosing a path:
Jumping randomly into the hottest trend, crypto today, options tomorrow, forex next week. This approach often results in shallow knowledge and limited progress across all areas.
Waiting too long to “find the perfect style”, endlessly researching but never actually starting.
Both approaches can lead to frustration and stalled development. The reality is simple: there is no “best” path, only the one that matches current goals, lifestyle, and learning stage.
Key Insights Here are three essential lessons to keep in mind when making this crucial choice.
Lifestyle dictates the appropriate path. If we have a full-time job, day trading may not be realistic, swing trading or long-term investing might fit much better. Conversely, if we love analyzing numbers daily, short-term trading could provide the engagement we need to stay motivated and focused.
Risk tolerance sets natural boundaries. Some paths like options or futures use leverage and higher volatility that can amplify both gains and losses. If losing 20% in a week would be paralyzing, starting with lower-risk vehicles like ETFs or blue-chip stocks makes more sense for building confidence.
The chosen path will inevitably evolve. Many successful traders started with one style, then pivoted as they gained experience and confidence. The key is starting with a path that matches our current readiness rather than jumping to advanced strategies too quickly.
Closing Thought The fork in the road is not a trap but an invitation to begin the journey. There’s no need to see the entire path ahead. Just choose one direction and walk it with focus and commitment.
Every path has its value and learning opportunities. What matters is taking action and learning through practice. As experience accumulates and understanding deepens, traders naturally know when to adjust direction or expand into new areas.

title: Step 5: Decision & Risk Management
description: Analysis isn't a decision. How to turn a bull/bear synthesis into an actual position size, entry plan, and exit strategy, with a reusable checklist so every future decision goes through the same discipline.
content:
Most investors can analyze reasonably well and still struggle at exactly this step: “I’ve done all this work. Now what?” A simple buy/sell/hold rating is incomplete. It doesn’t say how much to buy, when to sell, or how risk gets managed along the way. A professional decision always answers five questions:
Do I invest? (Yes / No / Wait) How much? (Position size, as a percentage of the portfolio) When? (Now, scale in, or wait for a specific entry point) Exit plan? (Stop-loss, profit target, or time limit) Monitoring? (What you’ll track, and how often) The gap between “NVIDIA is a buy” and “NVIDIA is a buy at a 5% position size, scaled in between $450–500, exit if margins fall below 65% or the stock drops 20%, with profits taken starting at $650” is the entire difference between an amateur decision and a professional one.
Position sizing: conviction times risk/reward Position size should reflect two inputs together, not either alone. High conviction without a favorable risk/reward can mean overconfidence; a favorable risk/reward without real conviction can mean you’re missing something. Both together justify a larger position:
High conviction + favorable risk/reward → 10-15% position High conviction + mixed risk/reward → 7-10% position Medium conviction + favorable risk/reward → 5-7% position Medium conviction + mixed risk/reward → 3-5% position Low conviction (any risk/reward) → 0-2% position, or pass The prompt template to generate a recommendation:
Based on the following analysis of [COMPANY]: **Bull Case**: [Summary - upside potential, probability] **Bear Case**: [Summary - downside risk, probability] **Current Conviction Level**: [High/Medium/Low] **My Risk Tolerance**: [Conservative/Moderate/Aggressive] **Portfolio Context**: [Total portfolio size, existing positions, sector exposure] Recommend: 1. Appropriate position size (% of portfolio) 2. Rationale for this sizing 3. Is this a core holding or satellite position? 4. Should I enter all at once or scale in? For a bull/bear synthesis on NVIDIA showing medium conviction and a slightly unfavorable risk/reward at the current price, this produces a specific, defensible number. Not “moderate,” but something like 3–5% of the portfolio, entered in two tranches (an initial position now, the remainder added only if the stock pulls back toward a defined support level).
Setting the exit before you enter The single habit that separates disciplined investing from hoping is defining the exit before buying, not after:
Design exit triggers for my [COMPANY] investment: **Investment Thesis**: [One-sentence summary of why you own it] **Key Bull Dependencies**: [What has to stay true for thesis to work] **Key Bear Risks**: [What would invalidate the thesis] Provide: 1. **Fundamental Exit Triggers**: What business metrics or events would signal thesis is broken? 2. **Technical Stop-Loss**: What price level represents unacceptable loss? (typically 15-25% down) 3. **Time-Based Review**: When should I reassess if nothing changes? (e.g., 6 months) 4. **Take-Profit Strategy**: At what price should I take partial profits? 5. **Trailing Stop**: Should I use a trailing stop as the stock rises? A complete exit plan has two independent halves. The downside side is a technical stop-loss (typically 15–25% below entry) plus named fundamental triggers, for example “exit if revenue growth falls below 20% year-over-year” or “exit if gross margin drops below 65%.” They should be specific enough that you can check them mechanically at each earnings release, not vague enough to argue your way around later. The upside side is a laddered take-profit plan: selling a third of the position at one target, another third at a higher one, and letting the remainder run if the thesis is still intact. That locks in gains without forcing you to guess the exact top.
Common position-sizing guidelines As a general (not universal) framework:
Core holdings (high conviction, low risk): 8-15% per position Growth holdings (high conviction, higher risk): 5-10% per position Speculative holdings (medium/low conviction): 2-5% per position Experimental/learning holdings: 1-2% per position Maximum per sector: 25-30% Maximum per single stock: 15-20% And a few risk-management defaults worth adopting as habits: a stop-loss 15–25% below entry, taking 25–50% of profits off the table at a 2x gain and letting the rest run, trimming any position that’s grown past roughly 20% of the portfolio back toward 15%, and never risking more than 2–3% of total portfolio value on a single trade going wrong.
The document that ties it together: an investment memo After going through this process, write it down in a one-page memo. Future you will forget today’s reasoning, and documentation is what lets you actually learn from outcomes later instead of rewriting history in hindsight.
INVESTMENT MEMO: [Company] Date: Current Price: DECISION: POSITION SIZE: INVESTMENT THESIS (one sentence): BULL CASE: [upside, probability] BEAR CASE: [downside, probability] BASE CASE: [most likely outcome, probability] ENTRY STRATEGY: EXIT TRIGGERS (technical + fundamental): KEY METRICS TO MONITOR: NEXT REVIEW DATE: What AI can and can’t do here AI is genuinely useful for structuring the decision framework, calculating position sizes from parameters you supply, suggesting exit triggers grounded in your own stated thesis, and running scenario analysis. It cannot tell you your personal risk tolerance, predict the future with certainty, or make the final call. That responsibility, deliberately, stays with you.
A reusable checklist for every future decision Run every investment through the same short gate before committing capital:
I can state my thesis in one clear sentence I’ve generated and taken seriously both a bull case and a bear case I’ve assigned rough probabilities to bull / base / bear outcomes My position size reflects both conviction and risk/reward, not conviction alone I have a stop-loss, a profit-taking plan, and named fundamental exit triggers, defined before entry I know what I’m monitoring, and on what schedule I’ve written a one-page memo I could hand to someone else and have them understand the decision If you’d be uncomfortable explaining this decision to another person, or if you find yourself unable to answer “what would make me sell,” that’s a signal to slow down before you act, not after.
Good process doesn’t guarantee a good outcome on any single trade. Even a well-run process is happy with a win rate in the 55–60% range over time. What it guarantees is that your decisions are repeatable, reviewable, and improvable, which is the entire point of running an analysis this way instead of on gut feel.
The final article in this series pulls the full five-step workflow back together, covers the mistakes that undo even a good process, and lays out a concrete plan for practicing it on your own.

title: Trading Math Made Simple: Compounding, Risk & Leverage
description: Master the mathematical foundations of compounding growth, position sizing, and leverage management essential for long-term trading survival.
content:
Every explorer needs survival tools. In trading, math is our compass, rope, and shield.
Introduction Imagine this scenario: someone makes a few winning trades, their account grows, and they start dreaming of doubling it every month. But without proper risk management, one bad trade wipes out weeks of progress, or worse, their entire account due to oversized bets.
This is where most beginners discover the harsh truth: trading isn’t just about charts and news. It’s about math. The numbers behind compounding, risk, and leverage quietly determine whether we will survive long enough to succeed.
These mathematical tools are like learning to read a map, tie essential knots, and check our equipment before venturing deep into the trading wilderness.
The Challenge Many new traders fall into the same mathematical traps:
They ignore compounding by chasing huge wins instead of small consistent growth. They misjudge risk by betting too much on one trade. They abuse leverage by thinking of it as “free money” instead of a double-edged sword.
Beginners often confuse probability with certainty. They might think: “If I win 70% of the time, I’ll always make money” or “If I just use more leverage, I’ll get rich faster.”
But the math doesn’t lie. Even a few small mistakes can sink the ship completely.
Key Insights Here are the three fundamental mathematical concepts that govern trading success.
Compounding: Creating the Snowball Effect
Compounding creates the snowball effect that builds wealth over time. This happens when profits are reinvested, creating growth on top of growth. For example, $10,000 growing at just 2% per month for 5 years becomes $32,800 without any additional deposits. This growth requires no additional capital injection, purely from reinvestment of profits.
The more important insight is that consistency beats speed. Traders pursuing monthly doubling often take excessive risks, resulting in account wipeouts during market corrections. Those pursuing steady, small gains through compounding often outperform profit-chasers in the long run.
Risk Management: The Survival Shield
Risk management acts as the survival shield that keeps us in the game. Risk per trade should usually be 1–2% of the account. This percentage may seem conservative, but it’s the standard widely adopted by professional traders.
The mathematical logic is simple: if risking 10% per trade, 10 consecutive losses will cause account blowup. If risk is controlled at 1%, even 20 consecutive losses still preserve about 82% of the account. We don’t go broke solely from losing trades but from bad risk management, which allows losses to compound destructively.
Leverage: The Double-Edged Sword
Leverage is a double-edged sword that can accelerate both success and failure. Leverage allows controlling more with less (e.g., 10:1 leverage means $1,000 controls $10,000). The upside is that small moves equal big profits. The downside is that small moves equal big losses.
The key is understanding that leverage is essentially an amplifier. Used wisely, leverage magnifies compounding effects. Used recklessly, it accelerates complete ruin.
Closing Thought Trading math isn’t about being a genius. It’s about equipping ourselves with the right survival tools. The moment we master these mathematical instruments, we stop wandering lost in the market jungle and start navigating like seasoned explorers.
